html:
The Karankawa were Indigenous peoples of the Gulf coast of Texas, around Galveston and Matagorda bays and the lower Colorado and Brazos river valleys. They were several independent bands that shared a language and much of their culture.

They moved with the seasons, between camps on the bays and barrier islands, where they lived on fish and shellfish, and the land inland, where they hunted deer and bison and gathered plants. They travelled the lagoons in dugout canoes and were noted archers.

They appear early in European records. In 1528 the shipwrecked Spaniard Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca lived among coastal peoples here, probably including Karankawa bands. In 1685 the French explorer La Salle built Fort Saint Louis on their land; they destroyed it a few years later. Relations with the Spanish turned hostile after a Spanish ambush near the Presidio La Bahía in 1722.

In the 1820s Anglo settlers under Stephen F. Austin set out to drive them off, in clashes such as the Skull Creek massacre and the Battle of Jones Creek in 1824. By the 1840s the survivors had split; some went to Padre Island, others to Tamaulipas in Mexico. They were last recorded as a people around 1858. Their neighbours included the Tonkawa and the Coahuiltec.
sum: The Karankawa were Indigenous peoples of the Gulf coast of Texas, around Galveston and Matagorda bays and the lower Colorado and Brazos river valleys. They were several independent bands that shared a language and much of their culture.
